scenes.title: The problem: a flag nobody acts on is unrecovered revenue
scenes.subtitle: Revenue leakage hides in millions of billing events — at telco scale, even the 1.7% fraud rate in this course's real dataset quietly drains millions. A model can flag a transaction, but acting on the flag needs judgment, evidence-gathering, and for anything consequential a human in the loop.
scenes.say: Revenue leakage hides in millions of billing events. At telco scale, even the one point seven percent fraud rate in this course's real dataset quietly drains millions — and a fraud flag nobody acts on is simply unrecovered revenue. A model can raise the flag, but acting on it needs judgment, evidence gathering, and, for anything consequential, a human in the loop. This is course two-oh-two: a classic machine-learning pipeline builds the model, the platform serves it, and a decision agent consumes it — with a human-approval gate that we prove works in both directions.

scenes.title: Inside the machine: factory, tool, gate
scenes.subtitle: Build: a five-step pipeline trains, evaluates and registers the model, then stages it to object storage. Use: KServe serves it; a LangGraph agent consumes it as one tool among several. Act: a human-approval gate, proven in both directions, audited in Experiments.
scenes.say: The three loops here: build, use, act. The pipeline is the factory — load, preprocess, train, evaluate, register — and the staged artifact lands in object storage with full lineage. K serve then serves it over the V two protocol, and a Lang-graph agent consumes it as one tool among several: score the case, gather context, decide the route. And on anything consequential, the graph stops cold at a human-approval gate — a gate we prove both parked and approved, with the audit trail to show who did what.

scenes.tab: Solution shape · a classic-ML model as a governed agent tool
scenes.caption: A LangGraph agent (score → context → decide) consumes the fraud model as a KServe tool, grounds the case with Feast features, reasons with vLLM, stops at a human-approval gate, and audits every case to MLflow.
scenes.say: Here is the shape of the solution. At the center is the fraud-triage agent, a small Lang-Graph state machine running as a disposable pod. It does not contain the fraud model; instead it consumes the classic model as a tool, served on K-Serve. Its loop is score, then context, then decide: it scores the transaction with the model, grounds the case with billing features from the feature store, and reasons over both with the cluster's own language model. For anything consequential it stops at a human-approval gate, and every case is audited to M-L-flow. The classic model gives the number, the agent gives the judgment, and a human signs off. Let's walk the platform pieces that make it real.

scenes.tab: Data Science Pipelines · Run graph · the model factory
scenes.caption: load-data → preprocess → train → evaluate → register, every stage green. What the notebooks did cell by cell now runs as a Data Science Pipeline (KFP v2) on our reference cluster, Venice.
scenes.say: Here is the model factory, live on our reference cluster, Venice. What the original revenue-assurance notebooks did cell by cell now runs as a proper Data Science Pipeline: load a million billing records, preprocess them, train a Balanced Random Forest, evaluate it on a held-out split, and register the result. Every stage is a discrete, observable step, and the whole graph completed green in about two minutes. This is the difference between a model someone once trained and a model your platform can rebuild on demand, the same way, every time.

scenes.tab: Develop & train · Experiments · the registered training run
scenes.caption: The register stage lands in MLflow with full lineage · fraud-class F1 0.998, ROC-AUC ~1.0 on 300,000 held-out rows · and registers revassurance-fraud-brf v1, the version the agent will consume.
scenes.say: And the pipeline's register stage lands the run in M L flow with complete lineage. Read the metrics: fraud-class F-one of nought-point-nine-nine-eight, and R O C-A-U-C essentially one, measured on three hundred thousand held-out rows. The parameters record exactly how it was made — a Balanced Random Forest, one hundred estimators, trained on the published revenue-assurance dataset, through data-science-pipelines on K F P version two. And on the right, it registers revassurance-fraud-b-r-f, version one — the exact version the agent's scoring node will consume. Lineage is not paperwork here; it is the contract between the factory and the agent.

scenes.tab: Model registry · Version promotion · the governed handoff
scenes.caption: The registered fraud model is promoted through the registry · the explicit, governed step that decides which version the serving layer and the agent are allowed to use.
scenes.say: Before the agent can use it, the registered model is promoted through the registry — the explicit, governed handoff you see here. This is the control point that decides which version the serving layer, and therefore the agent, is actually allowed to consume. In a fraud system this governance is not optional: you must be able to say precisely which model made which decision, and to roll forward or back deliberately. The registry makes that a first-class, auditable action rather than a file copied into a bucket.

scenes.tab: Model serving · KServe deployment · the model as a tool
scenes.caption: The promoted version is served on KServe. This is pattern 2: the fraud model is a network endpoint the agent calls as a tool · never embedded in the agent pod.
scenes.say: The promoted version is then served on K-Serve, shown here as a live model deployment. This is the pattern-two lesson made concrete: the fraud model is a network endpoint, a tool the agent calls, never a library baked into the agent pod. The agent's LangGraph state machine has a scoring node that calls this endpoint, gathers billing context for non-trivial scores, and then decides — clear and hold cases complete autonomously, while the escalate path hits a human-approval gate that checkpoints and pauses until a person approves. The model scores; the agent reasons; the human approves. Each of those is a separate, swappable, observable piece of the platform.

scenes.tab: The agent, live · the approval gate proven both ways
scenes.caption: A live triage case on Venice: the served model scored it 1.0, policy escalated it, the LangGraph gate checkpointed, and the audit run records decision, outcome, decided-by, approval-required, and the approver's identity · the whole decision reconstructable from platform data.
scenes.say: And here is the agent itself, live on the cluster, with the proof that matters most. Each triage case is an audited run in the same experiment that trained the model. This one: the served model scored the case at probability one, the policy rail escalated it, and the Lang-Graph gate did something a prompt never could — it checkpointed the graph mid-case and stopped. We ran it both ways. Without a human approval, both escalations simply parked as awaiting-approval; nothing proceeded. With an approval, the graph resumed and the approver's identity landed in the audit record you see here: decision, outcome, who decided, and who approved — the entire decision reconstructable from platform data alone. The model scores, the agent reasons, and a human approves. That is the whole lesson of two-oh-two, running for real.

scenes.title: 202, solved: the pipeline is the model's factory, the agent is its consumer
scenes.subtitle: A repeatable, per-stage-observable pipeline registers a versioned model; the registry governs the handoff; KServe serves it; and a LangGraph agent consumes it as a tool with human approval on the risky path. Classic ML as an agent tool, never the decision itself on high-risk cases. Next: 301 closes the loop · agents that don't just decide, but act, under governance. Replay every step yourself in the self-service interactive lab — a time-snapshotted capture of this same cluster — linked from the course page.
scenes.say: So that's two-oh-two, solved. A repeatable, per-stage-observable pipeline is the model's factory; it registers a versioned model; the registry governs the handoff; K-Serve serves it; and a LangGraph agent consumes it as a tool, with a human approval gate on the high-risk path. The classic model is an input to reasoning, never the final decision on a case that matters. From here, course three-oh-one raises the stakes again: agents that do not just decide, but act on the network — under governance. Thanks for watching. And you do not have to take this video's word for any of it: the course page links a self-service interactive lab, a time-snapshotted replay of this very cluster, where you run every step and verify every value yourself.
